editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The generalized Petersen graph \(G(n,k)\) is a cubic graph with vertex set \(V(G(n,k))=\{v_i\}_{0 \leq i < n} \cup \{w_i\}_{0 \leq i < n}\) and edge set \(E(G(n,k))=\{v_i v_{i+1}\}_{0 \leq i < n} \cup \{w_i w_{i+k}\}_{0 \leq i < n} \cup \{v_i w_i\}_{0 \leq i < n}\) where the indices are taken modulo \(n\). Schwenk found the number of Hamiltonian cycles in \(G(n,2)\), and in this article we present initial conditions and linear recurrence relations for the number of Hamiltonian cycles in \(G(n,3)\) and \(G(n,4)\). This is attained by introducing \(G'(n,k)\), which is a modified version of \(G(n,k)\), and a subset of its subgraphs which we call admissible, and which are partitioned into different classes in such a manner that we can find relations between the number of admissible subgraphs of each class. The classes and their relations define a directed graph such that each strongly connected component is of a manageable size for \(k=3\) and \(k=4\), which allows us to find linear recurrence relations for the number of admissible subgraphs in each class in these cases. The number of Hamiltonian cycles in \(G(n,k)\) is a sum of the number of admissible subgraphs of \(G'(n,k)\) over a certain subset of the classes.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: With regard to the Hadwiger-Nelson problem, several 5-chromatic unit distance graphs in the Euclidean plane have been discovered in recent years. While most constructions rely heavily on the Moser spindle, a few recent examples completely avoid it, the smallest one consisting of 1441 vertices. In this note, we introduce an original geometric approach to constructing such graphs by utilizing the arcs of a 7-fold symmetric unit distance graph on 21 vertices, and obtain a Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic unit distance graph on 2131 vertices. While this is not a record small result, it arises from a straightforward, structured rule rather than a purely automated or brute-force search.

title.title: A Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic unit distance graph on 2131 vertices in the plane

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Bent functions are Boolean functions that are maximally nonlinear. They can be represented as bent squares, i.e., square matrices for which each row and each column is the Walsh spectrum of a Boolean function. Using this representation, it is shown in this note that the number of bent functions in $n$ variables is at least $2^{n \cdot 2^{\frac{n}{2}} \left(1 + O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right)}$ for even integers $n$.

title.title: A lower bound on the number of bent squares

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Hexastix is an arrangement of non-overlapping infinite hexagonal prisms in four different directions that cover $\frac{3}{4}$ of space. We consider a possible generalization to $n$ dimensions, based on the permutohedral lattice $A^*_n$. The central lines of the generalized prisms are going to be oriented in $n+1$ different directions (parallel to the shortest non-zero vectors of $A^*_n$). The projection of the lines oriented in any direction along that direction to a hyperplane perpendicular to it is required to be a translation of the corresponding projection of $A^*_n$, and the minimal distance between lines oriented in any two given directions should be maximal. It is shown that this is possible if $n$ is a prime power. Also, the proportion of $n$-space that is covered is calculated for $n \in \{4, 5\}$, and an alternative generalization is briefly considered.

msc.text: Combinatorial aspects of packing and covering

title.title: A generalization of the hexastix arrangement to higher dimensions

editorial_contributions.text:
Given any positive integer \(n\), consider partitions of the set \(\{1, 2, 3, \dots, 2n\}\) into two disjoint classes \(\{a_i\}\) and \(\{b_j\}\) with \(n\) elements in each class. Let \(M_k\) denote the number of solutions of \(a_i- b_j= k\). Let \(M(n)= \min \max_k M_k\) where the minimum is taken over all partitions. To estimate \(M(n)\) is the minimum overlap problem introduced by \textit{P. Erdös} [Riveon Lematematika 9, 45-48 (1955); Colloque Théorie des Nombres, Bruxelles 1955, 127-137 (1956; Zbl 0073.03102)]. It is known that \(0.3564\leq \lim M(n)/ n\leq 0.4\). As to the upper bound, see \textit{T. S. Motzkin}, \textit{K. E. Ralston} and \textit{J. L. Selfridge} [Bull. Am. Math. Soc. 62, 558 (1956)]. 


In the paper under review the author improves the upper bound to 0.3857. A crucial conjecture of the author is proved by P. Swinnerton-Dyer and his proof is reproduced in the paper. This result allows the further improvement to 0.3821.

title.title: Advances in the minimum overlap problem

editorial_contributions.text: Paul Erdös has made the following conjecture: There exists a positive number \(M\) and an infinite sequence \((\gamma_j)_{j= 1}^\infty\) of Gaussian primes such that \(|\gamma_1|\leq M\), \(|\gamma_{j+ 1}-\gamma_j|\leq M\) for all \(j\), and \(\lim_{j\to \infty}|\gamma_j|= \infty\). The author gives an elementary argument rendering the plausibility of the analogous conjecture for the Eisensteinian primes questionable.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: Two conjectures about twin primes and primes of the form \(n^ 2+1\) are stated and supported by numerical evidence. According to the first conjecture each interval of the form \([n(n-1)/2+1,n(n+1)/2]\) contains at least one \(v\) such that \(6v-1\) and \(6v+1\) are prime numbers, and according to the second conjecture, each such interval will also contain a \(u\) such that \(4u^ 2+1\) is a prime.

title.title: Yet another hypothesis on classical prime number problems

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: It is conjectured that for each even number \(2n>6\) there exist a prime \(p\) such that \(2n-p\) is also a prime, and a prime \(p\) such that \(2n+p\) is also a prime, and in both cases such that \(p<(C_ 2)^{-1}(\ln(2n))^ 2\ln\ln (2n)\), where \(C_ 2=\prod_{p>2} p(p-2)(p-1)^{-2}= 0.66016\ldots\). The conjecture has been checked by computer and found to hold for \(2n\leq 5\cdot 10^ 6\).
